explanation_en: Risk shifting refers to using derivatives (eg, forward commitments, contingent claims) to modify risk by moving exposure to a counterparty. Forward commitments (eg, futures, forwards, swaps) do not require a premium payment at initiation but obligate both parties to complete the transaction in the future (Choice C). The futures contract specifies the price of the commodity in the future, and thus eliminates the price uncertainty and limits the risk for the company purchasing the commodity. The risk is shifted to the counterparty in the futures contract. (Choice B) Risk shifting can also be achieved by using contingent claims (eg, options). In contrast to forward commitments, options require the buyer to pay a premium. The advantage of paying the premium is that the buyer is granted the right, but not the obligation, to exercise the option.

question_en: Which of the following is most accurate with regard to a dual-class share structure?
option_a: Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of ownership.
option_b: It may grant founders superior voting control even if their ownership level falls below 50%.
option_c: It typically grants outside shareholders greater voting power than insiders and family
explanation_en: Normally, public companies have a share structure that grants each shareholder proportional voting power based on the number of shares held. For example, a shareholder who owns 50% of the company controls 50% of the votes. One exception to the general rule is a dual-class structure, where different share classes allow different numbers of votes per share (eg, Class A at one vote per share vs. Class B at two votes per share). A dual-class structure may create disproportional voting power relative to share ownership. Insiders (eg, founders) commonly hold Class B shares, which grant them dominant voting control on important issues (eg, board elections or strategic decisions) even if their share ownership falls below 50%. (Choice A) Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of share ownership only if all shares grant the same number of votes. Different share classes allow for different votes per share in a dual-class structure. (Choice C) Class B shares are granted mainly to insiders and family members and not to outside shareholders; therefore, greater voting power is typically held by insiders and family members.

question_en: A company's analyst made the following after-tax cash flow projections for two independent investments: The cost of capital is the company's hurdle rate of 12.5%. Based on the internal rate of return (IRR) approach, which of the following actions is most appropriate for the company?
option_c: Invest in both Projects A and B.
explanation_en: Companies often make choices among possible projects since there are constraints that prevent them from pursuing all net present value (NPV) positive projects. Depending on the circumstances, these project interactions include: project sequencing, capital rationing, or mutually exclusive projects. With project sequencing, projects are lined up sequentially through time, so that investing in Project X creates the option to invest in Project Y. The decision to invest in Project Y (or other future projects) will be based on the completion and success of Project X. For example, a company may begin delivery services in a new region. Depending on the success of the delivery service, the company will decide whether to build a distribution center in that region. (Choice A) Capital rationing is the process of allocating limited resources (at any one time) to the most profitable combination of projects. This occurs when a company has more positive NPV projects than its resources will allow it to pursue. (Choice B) Mutually exclusive projects are those that compete directly with each other, so only one project can be selected. This is usually due to a resource constraint.

question_en: A project has the following forecasted annual cash flows (in ¥ billions): Based on this information, which of the following discount rates will produce the lowest net present value (NPV)?
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
The net present value (NPV) of an investment equals the present value of its forecasted net cash flows (ie, inflows minus outflows). The discount
rate used for calculating NPV is the required rate of return for investors, which accounts for the investment's risk.
Typically, for projects with conventional cash flows (ie, one initial negative cash flow followed by positive future cash flows), lower discount rates
will yield higher NPVs. However, for projects with unconventional cash flows (ie, negative cash flows occurring beyond the initial period), the
relationship between discount rates and the size of the NPV can vary.
In this case, the investment has unconventional cash flows. The lowest discount rate (6%) yields the lowest NPV (−¥0.52 billion) (Choices B and
C). This occurs because the sizable negative terminal cash flow generates the most negative present value when using the 6% discount rate;
therefore, the NPV is reduced more than under the other two rates.

With project sequencing, the ability to start a project is contingent on the completion of another project. For example, the second version of
a device will start production only after the first version of the device proves its potential.
(Choice A) If two projects are mutually exclusive, then only one can be selected. For example, a company with financing to bring only one
gaming device to market would have to choose between two prototypes in development.
(Choice B) Even when a company has access to unlimited funding, projects with negative NPVs should be rejected since they destroy wealth.

question_en: A corporation is evaluating two projects with the following cash flows (INR million): Project 1 has a required rate of return of 3% and an internal rate of return (IRR) of 26.9%, while Project 2 has a required rate of return of 8% and an IRR of 38.8%. If the projects are mutually exclusive, the most appropriate investment decision is to invest in:
explanation_en:
HP 12c TI BA II Plus
Net present value (NPV) analysis evaluates investments based on the present value of a project's cash flows. NPV is the difference between
the present values of the project's cash outflows and inflows. The projected cash flows are discounted to the present using the required rate
of return (r) as the discount rate. As a result, projects with a positive NPV add to company value.
Project 1 is the most appropriate investment choice in this scenario since it has a higher NPV than Project 2 and will therefore add more
shareholder value to the corporation.
(Choice B) Project 2 seems to be the better choice based on its higher internal rate of return (IRR); however, the NPV is a superior decision
criterion since NPV measures the actual value added to the company, whereas IRR measures a percentage return. A project can have a higher
percentage return but a smaller NPV, based on the timing of the cash flows and their discount rate, resulting in less value added to the
corporation.
(Choice C) Since the projects are mutually exclusive, the corporation cannot invest in both projects, although each has a positive NPV and would
add value.

When making a capital investment decision, firms typically use the capital allocation process based on a cash flow analysis. Common capital

question_en: A company discloses its required depreciation expense for five years: The company uses units of production to calculate depreciation expense. Based only on this data, the company most likely expects an increase in:
explanation_en:
The units-of-production depreciation method expenses an asset's cost based on its use during each period. Depreciation expense is
calculated by multiplying the units produced each year by the depreciable unit cost, which is calculated as the asset's depreciable value (ie, initial
cost less salvage value) divided by the total number of units expected to be produced over the asset's life.
The depreciable unit cost is constant since the asset's cost is known, and the salvage value and the total number of units expected to be produced
are estimated at the beginning of the asset's life (Choice C). Therefore, the only variable that can change the depreciation expense will be the
actual number of units produced. Using the units-of-production method, if the depreciation expense increases each year, the number of units
produced is also expected to grow.
(Choice B) Net margin (ie, net profit margin) is a measure of profitability, and it increases only if profit increases or revenue decreases. In this
scenario, although production and COGS are expected to grow, that does not suggest the net margin will increase.

question_en: A company that reports under US GAAP decides to change its inventory accounting from FIFO to LIFO. The change on its financial statements is most appropriately disclosed:
option_a: retroactively, including a restatement of prior years' financial statements.
option_b: retroactively, without restating prior financial statements but disclosing the impact of the change to prior years' statements in footnotes.
option_c: prospectively, without restating prior financial statements but disclosing the impact of the
explanation_en: Inventory constitutes a large percentage of total assets for many companies and can significantly impact revenue, expenses (ie, cost of sales), and liquidity. As such, companies provide inventory-related disclosures in financial statements to better explain reporting methods and trends. One important category of disclosure relates to reversals of previously written down inventory, which is permitted under IFRS only. In general, a write-down occurs when an inventory item's market value falls below its carrying value on the balance sheet. A write-down increases expenses (cost of sales) and lowers profits. Any subsequent reversals of write-downs will allow companies to recapture these lost profits. (Choice A) LIFO reporting is allowed under US GAAP, not IFRS. LIFO reserves measure the difference between ending inventory value measured under FIFO and LIFO and are reported only for US GAAP companies. (Choice B) Companies using both US GAAP and IFRS disclose information related to inventory write-downs.

explanation_en:
Inventory may lose value due to spoilage, obsolescence, or declines in selling prices. Companies often update their inventory values on the
balance sheet to account for such events. US GAAP require companies to report inventory at the lower of historical cost or market value (MV).
When a company reports under US GAAP and uses LIFO as its inventory costing method, MV is the current replacement cost subject to an
upper and lower limit.
The upper limit is the net realizable value (NRV), which is the selling price net of the costs to complete and sell the inventory. In this
scenario, NRV = Selling price − Selling cost − Completion cost, so NRV = 140 − 10 − 30 = 100.
The lower limit is the NRV minus a normal profit margin. In this scenario, the lower limit is NRV − Normal profit margin = 100 − 7 = 93.
MV is always the middle number of the replacement cost (RC), upper limit, and lower limit when ranked in order:
If RC > Upper > Lower, MV is the upper limit.
If Upper > RC > Lower, MV is the RC.
If Upper > Lower > RC, MV is the lower limit.
In this case, the MV is the RC of $96 per unit since it is within the upper and lower limits and is lower than the historical cost of the inventory.
(Choice B) $100 is the upper limit for MV, which is capped at the upper limit only when RC exceeds the upper limit.
(Choice C) $105 is the company's historical cost. The inventory's NRV is lower than its historical cost, so the NRV should be reported.

question_en: A company that reports under IFRS is valuing its year-end inventory. It has collected the following information (in CHF millions): Based on this data, the inventory value (in CHF millions) reported on its balance sheet is closest to:
explanation_en:
Inventory is initially recorded on a company's balance sheet at historic cost. However, companies are required to regularly reassess this value. If
the inventory's value falls below its cost (eg, spoils, becomes obsolete, declines in selling price), the company must write down the inventory to
reflect the new, lower value, which becomes the carrying value.
IFRS require companies to report the carrying value of inventory at the lower of cost or net realizable value (NRV). The NRV is the estimated
selling price less the cost of completing and selling the inventory.
In this scenario, the NRV of the inventory is CHF 180 million (240 − 60). This is higher than the cost of 175, so no write down is taken and the
inventory remains at 175.
(Choice A) 165 is the replacement value, which is not used by IFRS in valuing inventory. The replacement value is used by companies reporting
under US GAAP and using LIFO or retail inventory methods when valuing inventory.
(Choice C) 180 is the NRV, which is greater than the historical cost. Since inventory is required to be valued at the lower of cost and NRV, the
company would not be permitted to increase the value of its inventory above 175.

explanation_en: A European put option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset at the exercise price on the date of the option's expiration. If the market price is less than the exercise price, then the put buyer has the right to sell the underlying asset at a higher price than the existing market price. The difference between the exercise price and the market price is the put buyer's payoff. If the market price is not lower than the exercise price, then the put buyer will not exercise the option, and there is no payoff. Therefore, the put buyer's payoff is the greater of (exercise price – market price) and zero. In this scenario, the put's exercise price at expiration is GBP 76, and the value of the underlying is GBP 83. The payoff is the greater of (76 – 83) = GBP −7 and zero, so the payoff is GBP 0. (Choice A) GBP −3 is the put buyer's profit, which equals the payoff minus the amount paid to purchase the option: (0 – 3) = GBP −3. (Choice C) GBP 7 is the result of subtracting the exercise price from the value of the underlying asset.
